issues.legal_issue: A breach of a mandatory requirement governing an execution-sale proclamation does not make the sale a nullity when the requirement protects only the judgment-debtor and the executing court has authority to sell the property.
material_facts: The sales occurred in execution of decrees concerning loans, and the executing court had authority to sell the attached properties.
The sale proclamations did not comply with the statutory requirements concerning the amount of property to be specified for sale and the minimum price.
The requirements were intended to protect the judgment-debtor’s private interests, and the judgment-debtor could waive that protection.
The court treated the requirements as mandatory for the purpose of deciding the appeals.
issues.conclusion: The non-compliance was an irregularity, not a nullity; the protection was for the judgment-debtor’s benefit and could be waived.
issues.legal_principle: The distinction between a nullity and an irregularity depends on the nature, scope, and object of the provision; a workable test is whether the objection can be waived. A mandatory provision may be waived when it exists solely for the private benefit of the person waiving it and no public interest is involved. The court relied on Ashutosh Sikdar v. Behari Lal Kirtania, Holmes v. Russell, the principles stated in Maxwell on the Interpretation of Statutes and Craies on Statute Law, A.L. Ar. Vellayan Chettiar v. Government of Madras, Gaya Prosad v. Seth Dhanrupwal Bhandari, Maniruddin Ahmed v. Umaprasanna, and Sheo Dayal Narain v. Musammat Moti Kuer. It considered section 35 of the Bengal Money-Lenders Act, 1940, alongside Order XXI, rules 64 and 66 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908.

rule.if: execution_sale_case and court_had_authority_to_sell and sale_requirement_was_breached and requirement_protected_only_private_interests and debtor_waived_protection

predicates.execution_sale_case: The matter concerns a sale of property in execution of a decree.
predicates.court_had_authority_to_sell: The executing court had authority to order the property sold.
predicates.sale_requirement_was_breached: The court conducted the sale without complying with a requirement governing the sale proclamation.
predicates.requirement_protected_only_private_inter: The breached requirement was intended solely to protect the private interests of the person affected, rather than a public interest.
predicates.debtor_waived_protection: The person for whose benefit the requirement existed relinquished the protection it provided.

issues.definition: When an execution sale is conducted by a court with authority to sell, breach of a requirement protecting only private interests, which the protected person waived, means the breach is an irregularity rather than a nullity.

issues.legal_issue: An execution sale cannot be set aside for an irregularity in its proclamation when the applicant did not preserve the objection after notice or has not sustained substantial injury because of the irregularity.
material_facts: The judgment-debtors applied under the civil procedure rule governing applications to set aside execution sales, relying in part on defects in the sale proclamations.
The judgment-debtors had received notice; one did not object to the valuation, and the other, despite filing valuation objections, did not attend when the proclamation was settled.
The lower courts concurrently found that the non-compliance caused no substantial injury to the judgment-debtor.
The subordinate judge found no fraud and found the prices obtained for the properties to be fair.
issues.conclusion: The sales could not be set aside under Order XXI, rule 90, because the applicants did not meet its requirements, including the requirement of substantial injury.
issues.legal_principle: Non-compliance with the sale-proclamation requirements is an irregularity in publishing or conducting the sale and is addressed through Order XXI, rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. Under that rule, an applicant must show substantial injury caused by the irregularity; a person who received notice but did not attend the drawing up of the proclamation, or who was present but did not object to the defect then, cannot seek to set the sale aside on that defect. The court approved Manindra Chandra v. Jagdish Chandra and Maniruddin Ahmed v. Umaprasanna, and distinguished Ashram Thikadar v. Vijay Singh Chopra.

rule.if: execution_sale_challenge and sale_proclamation_irregularity and ((notice_received and did_not_attend_proclamation) or (present_at_proclamation and no_objection_when_proclamation_set) or not substantial_injury_caused)

predicates.execution_sale_challenge: A person affected by an execution sale applied to have the sale set aside.
predicates.sale_proclamation_irregularity: The challenged sale involved an irregularity in the publication or conduct of the sale relating to its proclamation.
predicates.notice_received: The applicant received notice of the drawing up of the sale proclamation.
predicates.did_not_attend_proclamation: The applicant did not attend when the sale proclamation was drawn up.
predicates.present_at_proclamation: The applicant was present when the sale proclamation was drawn up.
predicates.no_objection_when_proclamation_set: The applicant did not object to the relied-on defect when the proclamation was drawn up.
predicates.substantial_injury_caused: The applicant sustained substantial injury because of the sale irregularity.

issues.definition: An execution-sale challenge based on a proclamation irregularity does not result in the sale being set aside when the applicant did not preserve the objection after notice or the irregularity caused no substantial injury.
